1939-08-23: Opening snapshot: the public nonaggression pact and secret allocation of spheres precede either invasion of Poland.
Diplomatic permission and territorial ambitions helped make aggression possible; a proposed sphere was not military control.
No invasion or October administration is projected onto this date. The secret protocol's approximate river references are not a surveyed frontier.
1939-09-01: Since 23 August, diplomacy has given way to Germany's invasion. The USSR has not yet invaded; Polish resistance continues at crossings and strongpoints.
The attack depended on intact bridges, communications and the ability to prevent Polish concentration. Orders and broad axes do not establish first-day reach.
Army arrows summarize operational directions. Read the dated engagement points for first-day events; the arrows are not daily tracks.
1939-09-17: Since 1 September, German advances have broken much of the Polish deployment. Soviet forces now invade from the east while Polish resistance and withdrawal continue.
The second invasion sharply narrowed opportunities to regroup or escape. Moscow's claim of protection was an official justification for aggression.
Soviet order arrows show assigned directions, not achieved movement. The later treaty boundary and November Soviet annexation claims do not belong to this snapshot.
1939-09-28: Since 17 September, the invaders have negotiated a revised division. Warsaw surrenders on this date, while Modlin, Hel and Polish forces in the Polesie sector still resist.
The new boundary agreement changes the August bargain. It does not extinguish Polish sovereignty or establish that fighting has ended everywhere.
The treaty line is distinguished from contemporary military presence. October German administrations are not backdated to September.
1939-10-26: Since 28 September, organized campaign resistance has ended and German civilian occupation administrations take effect. Claimed incorporations and the General Government are differentiated.
Administrative borders shaped coercion, property seizure, forced labour and displacement. Poland's recognized government continued abroad.
Łódź's later incorporation and the Soviet annexation acts of November are not projected backwards. Generalized regional outlines do not resolve every district.
1941-06-21: Opening Barbarossa snapshot: German and associated forces assemble before the invasion. The interval from October 1939 includes territorial changes that are explained separately, not animated.
Command sectors and transport corridors show the scale of preparation, while the studies connect operational planning to a war of conquest.
Sector markers are not headquarters coordinates. Preinvasion Soviet territorial claims, internationally contested sovereignty and German objectives remain distinct.
1941-06-22: Since 21 June, Germany has launched Barbarossa. Frontier penetrations, disrupted communications and local resistance coexist.
The first day's gains did not destroy the Soviet capacity to continue the war. Broken information complicated Soviet attempts to counterattack.
The reconstruction combines reports made at different times. An advance axis does not mean secure occupation of all ground behind it.
1941-06-25: Since 22 June, German mobile formations have advanced while Soviet armoured counterattacks develop in Lithuania and Ukraine. Finland enters open war with the USSR.
Local delays could matter without producing a coordinated recovery. In occupied Kaunas, anti-Jewish persecution escalated alongside the military advance.
The study includes reports from 23–24 June and later consequences. These are identified as context, not simultaneous unit observations.
1941-06-28: Since 25 June, the German encirclement around Białystok and Minsk has developed and Minsk has fallen. Resistance, escape and mass capture continue inside the affected region.
Closing the mobile arms of an encirclement did not instantly eliminate its defenders. Captivity and occupation exposed people to additional violence.
Pocket outlines are approximate operational envelopes; they do not count prisoners or locate every surviving unit.
1941-07-01: Since 28 June, the war has moved farther east at unequal speeds. Southern Soviet forces attempt fighting withdrawals; German troops enter Riga and occupy Lwów.
The struggle for routes and crossings interacted with the murder of prisoners and anti-Jewish violence in occupied cities.
Lwów's prison murders and the subsequent pogrom require separate perpetrators and chronology. A city locality marker does not identify each site of violence.
1941-07-03: Since 1 July, Stalin's public address accompanies reserve formation, evacuation and coercive mobilization. German and Romanian operations across the Prut widen the southern campaign.
Military resistance increasingly depended on moving people, industry and supplies. The study also explains the Iași massacre and negotiations for foreign aid.
Speeches and supply negotiations are explanatory context. A physical corridor does not establish a functioning supply service.
1941-07-06: Since 3 July, fresh Soviet mechanized forces attack towards Lepel and Senno as German troops approach the Dnieper–Dvina defensive region.
A large order of battle could not overcome failures of communication, concentration and supply. The counterstroke bought fighting time without recovering the frontier.
The selected view gives a regional relationship between forces; movements from subsequent days remain labelled context.
1941-07-09: Since 6 July, the Lepel counterstroke has failed to stop the German advance. German forces reach Pskov, Vitebsk and new southern approaches while Soviet formations continue to assemble.
A major frontier victory still fell short of a strategic decision. Longer distances and continued resistance increased the invader's obligations.
This closes an editorial phase, not the fighting. Loss figures in the study have their own definitions and intervals and are not map totals.
1941-07-10: Since 9 July, German crossings of the Dnieper open the approaches to Smolensk, while Soviet formations still defend other river sectors.
A crossed river was not a defeated defensive system. Reserves, bridges and interrupted railways shaped the next battle.
Reports from 10–12 July are distinguished in the study. Crossing locations and connecting operational edges have different precision.
1941-07-16: Since 10 July, German troops have entered Smolensk, but Soviet resistance continues in and around the city. The northern advance has also encountered the Soltsy counterstroke.
Entry into a city did not close its exits or end its defence. German occupation plans developed while the military outcome remained contested.
City capture, fighting and encirclement are separate claims. The reconstruction does not synchronize every report to one hour.
1941-07-23: Since 16 July, Soviet counterattacks around Smolensk bring additional reserves into battle, often before they can concentrate effectively.
Continued Soviet action imposed obligations on German forces whose mobile formations had outrun parts of their support.
Named attack sectors are supported more closely than connecting front lines. Mogilev and later outcomes in the study retain their component dates.
1941-07-30: Since 23 July, Germany's Directive No. 34 acknowledges the need to restore fighting power. Repair, transport and Soviet institutional recovery alter the campaign's timetable.
An operational pause was not inactivity across the entire front. The Polish–Soviet agreement and Hopkins's mission belong to the widening political war.
Diplomatic developments are context rather than troop positions. Railway connections do not establish restored capacity or converted gauge.
1941-08-06: Since 30 July, the encirclement at Uman has tightened around the Soviet 6th and 12th Armies. Attempts to break out continue under severe shortages.
The destruction of formations also meant captivity, wounded men left behind and new dangers for occupied communities.
The pocket is a generalized area, not a continuous surveyed ring. Later prisoner totals and the outcomes of individual escape attempts are not completed facts on 6 August.
1941-08-12: Since 6 August, fighting widens around Leningrad's approaches, Staraya Russa and Odessa. Soviet counterattacks and a port still connected by sea create different operational problems.
The invading armies had to defend vulnerable flanks and sustain longer communications while occupation violence spread.
Odessa's sea connection is distinct from an open land route. Schematic sea corridors do not establish a particular ship's voyage.
1941-08-19: Since 12 August, German forces have reached Gomel while Soviet troops withdraw and establish positions beyond the rivers.
The loss of a junction affected communications between theatres, but capture, evacuation and continued resistance followed different clocks.
The selected date does not imply that every part of the city and its approaches changed hands simultaneously.
1941-08-21: Since 19 August, Hitler's decision redirects German effort towards Ukraine. The ordered turn south precedes the full movement and its later outcome.
Strategic priorities competed with the time and resources needed to move formations. Soviet command orders combined resistance with coercion.
Planned objectives are optional and separately styled. The Kiev encirclement is not shown as already accomplished.
1941-08-25: Since 21 August, the turn south develops alongside renewed Soviet attacks in the centre and fighting from Lake Ilmen to Odessa.
The front remained a set of interdependent operations. Civilian flight, captivity and the murder of Jewish children at Bila Tserkva belong to the same period of occupation.
The phase boundary is editorial. Broader civilian and international context is retained without converting every passage into a dated event marker.
1941-08-26: Since 25 August, the crossing at Novgorod-Seversky opens a route behind the Soviet Dnieper defence.
Rivers and road connections made the German turn south possible while exposing the difficulty of moving Soviet armies and supplies.
A bridgehead denotes a local foothold, not secure possession of all intervening territory. Connecting routes are schematic.
1941-08-29: Since 26 August, Tallinn has fallen and the Baltic Fleet's evacuation faces minefields and air attack. Finnish advances alter the Karelian situation.
A lost port could still send ships to sea, with sharply unequal prospects for crews, troops and civilian passengers.
Naval passage, land control and escape are separate relationships. No single casualty total is implied by the corridor symbols.
1941-09-03: Since 29 August, Soviet attacks at Yelnya have failed to complete the encirclement ordered for this date; the German exit remains open.
Recovering ground and destroying the defending force were different objectives. German withdrawal later in the week is not backdated.
The study's attack orders, reports and subsequent outcome are distinguished. Approximate sectors do not locate every regiment.
1941-09-08: Since 3 September, German forces have taken Shlisselburg and cut Leningrad's land connection. Yelnya has been recovered by Soviet forces.
Leningrad's survival now depended on constrained lake communications, rationing and continuing defence rather than an open land corridor.
The siege's later hunger and mortality are context, not totals already reached. Lake links are schematic and vary by season.
1941-09-12: Since 8 September, the two German mobile arms threatening Kiev draw closer while Soviet command debates withdrawal and reinforcement.
Holding the city and preserving the field armies increasingly pulled in different directions.
The future closure of the pocket is not projected backwards. Forward reach and secure rear areas remain different categories.
1941-09-16: Since 12 September, German mobile forces have linked around the Kiev region, trapping major Soviet formations whose resistance and escape attempts continue.
Encirclement changed the defenders' communications and supply without immediately ending their ability to fight.

The operational ring is generalized. Hiiumaa is shown as Soviet-held following the October local chronology; a conflicting September naval entry is disclosed rather than plotted as an established bridgehead.
1941-09-19: Since 16 September, Soviet forces have left Kiev and German troops have entered the city, while fighting in the encirclement continues farther east.
The capture of the city and destruction of the field armies were separate processes. Occupation introduced new institutions of violence.
Kiev's entry date does not establish a civilian-administration transfer. Later explosions and massacres are not backdated.
1941-09-26: Since 19 September, the Kiev pocket has largely been destroyed, though individual escape and resistance continue. German forces prepare new operations.
A major operational victory consumed time and resources and exposed prisoners to lethal captivity.
German prisoner claims require their own reporting scope. The map does not convert them into verified Soviet losses.
1941-09-29: Since 26 September, German preparations for the Moscow offensive gather force. At Kiev, the Babyn Yar massacre begins on 29 September.
Military victory and mass murder were connected through the occupation, while distinct actions and institutions carried responsibility.
The two-day massacre is not a completed result on its first day. Hiiumaa follows the October local landing chronology, with a conflicting September naval entry explicitly qualified.
1941-09-30: Since 29 September, Guderian's southern thrust opens Operation Typhoon; the army group's main assault is still to follow on 2 October. The Babyn Yar massacre continues.
The offensive had staggered beginnings. A campaign-wide phase label does not mean that all sectors attacked at once.
The map combines regional situations with dated component events. Ordered Moscow objectives remain distinct from achieved movement.
1941-10-02: Since 30 September, Army Group Centre's main attack begins, widening the offensive against the Soviet armies west of Moscow.
German plans sought encirclement of the defending armies before a decisive advance on the capital.
Later pocket closures are not already complete. Reported sectors are more certain than connecting operational edges.
1941-10-07: Since 2 October, German mobile forces have closed encirclements around Vyazma and Bryansk. Fighting and breakout attempts continue within them.
The pockets disrupted Soviet defence while also tying down German formations needed for further movement.
Encirclement does not mean immediate surrender. Pocket outlines do not establish an impermeable perimeter or a final prisoner total.
1941-10-13: Since 7 October, German forces have moved towards the next defensive positions on Moscow's approaches while resistance continues in the pockets.
The apparent opening ahead depended on the survival and reorganization of Soviet forces and on German supply reaching the advance.
The study distinguishes command changes, defensive preparation and later outcomes. Road corridors remain schematic.
1941-10-16: Since 13 October, German pressure and Soviet evacuation decisions have brought crisis to Moscow. Odessa's evacuation marks a different transition in the south.
Civilian movement, industrial evacuation and military defence relied on many of the same constrained communications.
Evacuation orders and destinations do not prove an individual's journey. Later events in Moscow remain context.
1941-10-19: Since 16 October, Moscow's defence is reorganized under siege measures while German forces continue fighting on its approaches.
The defence involved command, coercion, labour and continuing reinforcements as well as prepared positions.
A state of siege is a legal and administrative measure, distinct from complete military encirclement of the city.
1941-10-24: Since 19 October, German advances in the south extend the occupation and approach further objectives in the Donbas and Crimea, while the Moscow battle continues.
Operations in separate theatres competed for strength and brought additional communities under occupation.
Military control does not establish the precise extent of civil administration. Later Rostov operations are explanatory context.
1941-11-02: Since 24 October, German forces have advanced unevenly in Crimea and towards Moscow while the offensive's ability to sustain movement declines.
Terrain, weather, supply and Soviet resistance interacted; no single cause explains the changing pace everywhere.
The selected date is not a uniform pause along the front. Siege positions and approximate connecting sectors retain separate precision notes.
1941-11-09: Since 2 November, German forces have taken Tikhvin, threatening Leningrad's remaining supply arrangements. Soviet counteraction is developing.
A railway junction mattered because the besieged city's food had to cross a constrained transport system.
Capture of a junction does not establish German operation of its railway. The later Soviet recovery is not shown as complete.
1941-11-14: Since 9 November, commanders prepare renewed attacks while fighting around Tikhvin, Moscow and the southern front continues.
The prospect of another offensive depended on depleted formations, weather and the ability of both sides to bring up reserves.
This editorial boundary precedes the renewed effort; it is not a ceasefire or a simultaneous change across all theatres.
1941-11-15: Since 14 November, the final offensive effort begins in stages north of Moscow. Other German formations are still preparing their attacks.
Operational opportunity remained local and temporary. The ability to threaten Moscow did not restore the means for a short decisive war.
The map shows command sectors and component intervals; the entire army group is not assumed to attack at one hour.
1941-11-18: Since 15 November, Guderian's southern pincer develops around an undefeated Tula while fighting widens north of Moscow.
Bypassing a defended city created exposed flanks and additional supply obligations. Orders concerning civilian shelter extended the violence behind the line.
Kashira and the later counterstroke are context where their dates fall after the snapshot. Tula is not shaded as captured.
1941-11-21: Since 18 November, German forces have captured Rostov while a Soviet offensive threatens the northern flank of the German advance.
A city victory could deepen an army's exposure. Rostov's first occupation brought robbery, shootings and anti-Jewish persecution.
The short occupation of 1941 is distinguished from the larger massacre of 1942. No later victim total is projected onto this date.
1941-11-24: Since 21 November, Klin has fallen and German forces threaten the northern Moscow approaches; Soviet armies retreat and reserves continue to assemble.
The apparent gap required exploitation by formations already stretched by resistance, distance and changing orders.
Retreat, reinforcement and planned objectives have different time ranges. Sector markers do not locate individual headquarters.
1941-11-28: Since 24 November, German troops have reached and crossed the Moscow–Volga Canal at Yakhroma. Soviet counterattacks and revised German orders limit the eastern foothold.
An intraday crossing could be tactically dangerous without becoming a secure operational breakthrough. Demolition also displaced local families.
The canal foothold is contested intraday reach. It is not secure end-of-day control, and route bends are not tactical tracks.
1941-11-29: Since 28 November, Soviet forces have recovered Rostov and German troops withdraw. Around Moscow, the offensive continues under increasing pressure.
Rostov's recovery exposed a command dispute and showed that German gains could be reversed before the wider Moscow counteroffensive.
The city recovery date and subsequent withdrawal towards the Mius are separate events. Testimony and later findings retain their own evidentiary limits.
1941-12-02: Since 29 November, German attacks around Moscow and Tula still achieve local penetrations but cannot turn them into a decisive result.
Offensive strength and the reserves needed to exploit gains no longer matched the objectives, while Soviet reinforcements arrived.
Later withdrawal decisions and counteroffensive outcomes remain context. Paper formation strength is not treated as present combat strength.
1941-12-05: Since 2 December, German offensive efforts have faltered and Kalinin Front begins counteroffensive operations. The broader Moscow attacks develop in stages.
The expectation of a short war has failed, while occupation, captivity and the danger to civilians continue.
This is the atlas's current endpoint. Tikhvin is not yet recovered, and later December advances are not projected backwards.
